content.overview: Sections 3–9 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 establish the statutory rules for communicating proposals, acceptances and revocations; determine when those communications become complete; prescribe the requirements for acceptance; recognise acceptance by performance in the statutory circumstances; and distinguish express from implied promises.
content.glance: Sections 3–9 answer three connected questions: how a proposal, acceptance or revocation is communicated; when the communication becomes complete against each party; and whether the statutory requirements for acceptance or a promise have been satisfied.

sections.heading: Section 3 — Communication of Proposals, Acceptance and Revocation
sections.body: Section 3 provides that communication of a proposal, acceptance or revocation is made by an act or omission of the relevant party that is intended to communicate it or has the effect of communicating it.

sections.heading: Section 4 — When Communication Is Complete
sections.body: Section 4 fixes separate completion points. A proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Acceptance is complete against the proposer when it is put into a course of transmission so as to be beyond the acceptor's power, and against the acceptor when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer. Revocation is complete against its maker when it is put into transmission so as to be beyond the maker's power, and against the person to whom it is made when it comes to that person's knowledge.

sections.heading: Sections 5–6 — Revocation of Proposals and Acceptances
sections.body: Section 5 addresses the point up to which a proposal or acceptance may be revoked by reference to the statutory completion rules. Section 6 identifies the statutory modes of revocation of a proposal: communication of notice of revocation; lapse of the time prescribed in the proposal or, where no time is prescribed, lapse of a reasonable time without communication of acceptance; failure by the acceptor to fulfil a condition precedent to acceptance; and death or insanity of the proposer where that fact becomes known to the acceptor before acceptance.

sections.heading: Sections 7–9 — Acceptance and Promises
sections.body: Section 7 requires acceptance to be absolute and unqualified and, unless the proposal prescribes a particular manner, to be expressed in a usual and reasonable manner. Section 8 recognises acceptance by performing the conditions of a proposal or accepting consideration offered with a proposal, in the statutory circumstances. Section 9 distinguishes express promises, where the proposal or acceptance is made in words, from implied promises, where it is made otherwise than in words.

sections.heading: Application Checklist for Sections 3–9
sections.body:
1. Identify the proposal, acceptance or revocation.
2. Identify the relevant act, omission, transmission and knowledge.
3. Apply section 4 to determine the completion point against each party.
4. If revocation is alleged, apply sections 5–6.
5. If acceptance is alleged, test section 7 and, where applicable, section 8.
6. If the promise is not expressed in words, consider section 9.
7. State the statutory consequence supported by the applicable provision.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Communication of a Proposal
examples.body: A proposes by letter to sell a house to B at a stated price. Under section 4, communication of the proposal is complete when B receives the letter.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Postal Acceptance
examples.body: B accepts A's proposal by a letter sent by post. Under section 4, communication of the acceptance is complete against A when the letter is posted and against B when the letter is received by A.

examples.title: Illustration 3 — Revocation
examples.body: A revokes a proposal by telegram. Under section 4, the revocation is complete against A when the telegram is despatched and against B when B receives it.

examples.title: Illustration 4 — Qualified Acceptance
examples.body: A proposal receives a reply that adds a qualification rather than giving an absolute and unqualified acceptance. The response must be tested against section 7 before treating it as an acceptance.

hypotheticals.question: A posts a proposal to B. B posts an acceptance. Before the acceptance reaches A, A sends a revocation. How should the issue be analysed?
hypotheticals.analysis: Do not decide the issue merely by asking which communication arrived first. Identify the relevant communication events, apply section 4 to determine when acceptance and revocation became complete against each party, and then apply section 5 to determine whether revocation was still legally possible.

hypotheticals.question: B replies to a proposal saying that B accepts only subject to an additional condition. Is that necessarily an acceptance under section 7?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 7 requires acceptance to be absolute and unqualified. The actual wording of the response must therefore be examined before treating it as acceptance.

distinctions.title: Acceptance under sections 3–9 vs negotiation or further proposal
distinctions.right: Response that does not amount to an absolute and unqualified acceptance

rows.right: Requires separate analysis of the actual communication

rows.left: Apply the statutory completion rules in section 4
rows.right: Determine what the communication actually conveys

rows.left: Acceptance may have the statutory effect provided by the Act
rows.right: Do not treat the response as acceptance unless the statutory requirements are satisfied

misconceptions.trap: Assuming that the first communication to arrive automatically determines the legal result.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the separate completion rules in section 4 to acceptance and revocation and determine completion against each party.

misconceptions.trap: Treating every response that expresses agreement as an acceptance.
misconceptions.correction: Section 7 requires acceptance to be absolute and unqualified; examine the actual terms of the response.

enhancement.definition: Sections 3–9 govern communication, completion and revocation of proposals and acceptances, the statutory requirements for acceptance, acceptance by performance in the statutory circumstances, and the distinction between express and implied promises.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The legal effect of a proposal, acceptance or revocation under sections 3–9 depends on the statutory communication and completion rules and on whether the requirements for acceptance or a promise are satisfied.
essentialIngredients: Identify the proposal, acceptance or revocation.
Identify the relevant communication event and the parties affected by it.
Apply section 4 to determine when communication is complete.
Apply sections 5–6 where revocation is in issue.
Apply section 7 where acceptance is in issue.
Apply section 8 where acceptance by performance is alleged.
Apply section 9 to classify a promise as express or implied.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Sections 3–9 form Chapter I of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Section 3 addresses how proposals, acceptances and revocations are communicated. Section 4 fixes the completion point of those communications against the relevant party. Section 5 links revocation of proposals and acceptances to those completion rules, while section 6 specifies the statutory modes of revocation of proposals. Section 7 requires acceptance to be absolute and unqualified. Section 8 recognises acceptance through performance of proposal conditions or acceptance of consideration in the statutory circumstances. Section 9 distinguishes express promises from implied promises.
examples: A proposes by letter to sell a house to B; apply section 4 to the point at which the proposal comes to B's knowledge.
B accepts A's proposal by post; apply the separate completion points in section 4 against A and B.
A revokes a proposal by telegram; apply section 4 to determine completion against A and B.
A response that adds a qualification must be tested against the absolute-and-unqualified requirement in section 7.
problemApplication: Identify every proposal, acceptance and revocation.
Record the relevant acts, omissions, dispatches, transmissions and points of knowledge.

Apply section 8 or section 9 only where their statutory conditions are relevant.

keyTakeaways: Section 4 does not use one completion rule for every party; acceptance and revocation have separate completion points against the relevant parties.
Section 7 requires acceptance to be absolute and unqualified.
Section 8 deals with acceptance by performance in the statutory circumstances.
Section 9 distinguishes express promises from implied promises.
The topic should remain confined to sections 3–9 unless another authority is directly relevant and separately verified.

notes: Sections 3–9 were checked against the official India Code Indian Contract Act, 1872 text.
Section 3 covers communication of proposals, acceptance and revocation by an act or omission intended to communicate or having the effect of communicating it.
Section 4 sets separate completion rules for proposals, acceptances and revocations and distinguishes completion against the proposer/maker from completion against the acceptor/recipient.
Section 5 addresses the point up to which proposals and acceptances may be revoked by reference to the statutory completion rules.
Section 6 specifies the statutory modes of revocation of proposals.
Section 7 requires acceptance to be absolute and unqualified and addresses the manner of acceptance.
Section 8 recognises acceptance by performance of proposal conditions or acceptance of offered consideration in the statutory circumstances.
Section 9 distinguishes express and implied promises.
